g.text: Split the name from the bytes - and the two stores have nothing in common
The same move UNIX makes: a path resolves to an inode, and the inode points at blocks scattered across the disk.
throughput-bound needs NO transactions at all
bytes at an offset in a packed file
Why they cannot share a store
One store would mean picking one engine for a
transactional 0.7 TB index and for 100 PB of
opaque immutable blobs - and being wrong for one.
What object storage gave up to get there
Giving up in-place mutation and low latency is exactly what buys a flat namespace, an
HTTP interface, and the freedom to pack bytes however durability prefers rather than
The arithmetic that rules out one file per object
Buying bigger drives adds bytes but NOT IOPS - capacity per drive has grown ~100x in
twenty years while random IOPS has barely moved. So you cannot afford one filesystem
file per object, and that single conclusion is what forces the packed-file design.
Two properties make all of this tractable: objects are IMMUTABLE (no partial update, so no concurrent-writer problem and no
re-replication for consistency), and the access pattern is WRITE ONCE, READ MANY (about 95% of operations are reads).
